title: Breaking And Entering: Cat Power Reflects On Bob Dylan’s Influence
summary: Ahead of her tour, Cat Power Sings Dylan, acclaimed American singer-songwriter Cat Power talks in retrospect about her lifelong admiration of Bob Dylan. She chats to Simon and Lauren about how growing up listening to Bob Dylan’s music fostered her songwriting style and how songs like ‘Mr Tambourine Man’ introduced to her a blend of punk's raw lyricism with softer melodies.
transcript:
Chan Marshall, who performs as Cat Power, spoke with Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler about her lifelong relationship with Bob Dylan’s music, ahead of her Cat Power Sings Dylan performance at Festival Hall in Melbourne. The conversation was broadcast on Triple R on 20 February 2025.

Host: You Are Free, the sixth studio album by Cat Power, aka Chan Marshall, came out this week, 22 years ago. Certainly always a good time to revisit that extraordinary record. More recently, Cat Power has spent a lot of time touring, not necessarily her own music specifically, but Bob Dylan’s 1966 Royal Albert Hall concert, the show that famously marked Dylan’s controversial shift to electric. For Cat Power, it connects directly back to her earliest memories of Bob Dylan’s music, watching how adults would argue about his songs at parties in Georgia in the 1970s. She has mentioned many times in interviews that she never had a favourite artist apart from Bob Dylan. Here she begins by describing her first encounter with the artist, where he started life as an enigma before he became an influence.

Chan: I met my mum and my dad when I was five. All the people that came with them when I met them, they were all musicians. I noticed the way they would act when a Bob Dylan song would come on at a party or the house or wherever we were. I noticed how people would behave differently. His songs reminded me somewhat of, it was familiar in the way of a fable.

What made me notice him was the way the adults behaved when his music came on. They would talk about him as if either he’d done something wrong or he was being criticised. I wasn’t sure, I didn’t understand why they were playing his music if they didn’t like the guy, or why were there so many opinions about this person? Because I didn’t understand what a good voice was or what a good lyric was. I didn’t understand the context of critiquing anything. I learned that people had a lot to say about Bob, and that kind of introduced me to my own curiosity.

I became curious about him because when it was Jimi Hendrix or David Bowie, you know, Ziggy Stardust, there was a lot of oohing and aahing. There wasn’t any kind of discrepancy or caution. I think I’ve gravitated to his songs because I felt like they were casting him as an underdog in some kind of way. But I didn’t understand until I was older that it was just sort of schools of thought, basically. I think some people preferred the rock and roll antics to the critical thinking poetry kind of thing, the beat sort of thing he was doing.

Host: What was the first sort of Dylan song or lyric that really spoke to you?

Chan: I think ‘Mr Tambourine Man’, because that song, again, I’ve never been tested for autism. I’m just saying this. I know that I’ve felt, and I know a lot of people that love music felt, now we have words like neurotypical and neurodivergent. But I know that for myself as a little girl, I really lived in songs. I really just felt whole in them. I could escape. It was very visual for me, colourful, blah, blah, blah.

The only reason I’m saying that is because songs play a really big, important— they’re almost like a family member to me. I haven’t met very many people who have that sort of neurological, psychological issue with music. I think the first one for me was ‘Mr Tambourine Man’. I felt like that was, and still is, the most transcendental. It feels like it is a photograph of a dream or fairy tale. In these fairy tales we write or have been written, they’re always gonna be great, like they’re gonna end up great. The fairy tale is gonna work out.

That’s the thing about ‘Mr Tambourine Man’, there’s some hardship there, but it really has this, you can almost taste it, [Unclear audio at 00:04:38–00:04:49]. It feels really sweet and believable, even though it’s so preposterous. It’s like he’s screaming from the earth, ‘Get me out of here’, you know what I mean?

Host: That’s beautifully categorised. There’s some magic in it, for sure.

Chan: I feel like Bob has that same jester-ish thing of, the king can’t be told the truth or he’ll get his head cut off. So it’s like, you want the truth in a riddle, you want it in a joke, a song, a dance. I’ve always felt like Bob has had that sort of magician way about his lyrics to sort of charm you into thinking properly about stuff, which is really a gift.

[Music]

Host: It’s a great cover that you do of ‘Mr Tambourine Man’. We’ve spoken in the past about your view that covers are a form of musical conversation, and that you said that covering other people’s songs can be for you like medicine. Can you maybe describe the conversation you’ve had with Dylan through covering his music, and how has his music been like medicine for you?

Chan: Oh man, so when I was in junior high, there was an English teacher who was the basketball coach, and that happened very frequently. My science teacher was the gym teacher. But anyway, [Unclear audio at 00:06:38–00:06:41]. I wanted to do a punk rock song, but I thought I can’t go too far outside of the conservatism. I thought, well, I’ll do this Bob Dylan song because nobody knows this song.

I thought if I did my report, if I spoke these words out to the class, it would be something different that maybe they would be interested in. I was about 12 years old. I did choose that song because of how I saw the caste system in the South. Like, oh, if you’re poor, you’re nothing. Doesn’t matter your colour, your ethnicity, nothing. If you’re poor, you’re nothing. Teachers don’t like you. No one likes you. It was all about being poor.

Everybody else was doing major pop songs from the time. MTV was huge. I feel like that’s the first time I ever covered Bob Dylan, just bringing his lyrics to a group of people who never would have wanted to listen to that kind of music or whatever. But obviously when I started playing guitar and started singing songs professionally, choosing to sing for 40 bucks a night and free food instead of working five jobs a week to pay my rent, I really enjoyed playing different covers [Unclear audio at 00:07:57–00:08:03]. I just thought, oh well, these are some of the songs I know. No one’s going to like the songs I’m going to sing. My songs are about committing suicide and fighting Satan and things that no one wants to hear about.

But if I sing this beautiful cover of Bob Dylan, ‘Moonshiner’, which to this day, I rarely hear that song, that recording. But if you played it for me right now, it would suspend time for me. I would be lost in whatever vortex he created. I do believe in songs being medicine, a prescription to sort of stop time, to heal something that’s a part of us all. I don’t know, some sort of transcendental again. He’s been around since I was little. Bob’s still kicking around on earth and still recording great records. I think I’ll always be covering Bob’s songs. I’m guessing.

[Music]

Host: It’s beautiful to hear you talking about that connection that you have with his music. To continue that idea of your covers being a form of conversation, there’s a balance, I suppose, with staying true to the original but also introducing your own narrative shift or style. One example that we can think of is ‘She Belongs to Me’, where you move the perspective of the narrator. Could you tell us a little bit about these creative choices and how you find a place within the songs?

Chan: Well, I think just because I happen to be born a female and am cis, I am straight and a woman, singing from a personal perspective of I’m singing about ‘she’, it does give a different angle to, I guess, the audience member and the listener.

For myself, I do feel like right now, I feel choked up thinking about the power that we as women have to have survived this crazy ride of a life. For all of us, all of us that are still standing and still getting through the quiet part, getting through the loud part, having to be louder than we want to be to get our point across to deaf ears our whole life. Singing this song, it really is so enormous how I feel. The room is huge with this feminine energy of just this divine creative energy.

When I hear Dylan singing, for example, that song ‘To Ramona’, when he’s singing that song, I don’t know if you know that song, when he’s singing to Ramona, as a teenage girl that brought me to my knees. To have a song explicitly in honour of a female was so empowering for me as a young girl. I’ve never heard no song by no man really eloquently and elegantly, with a ton of grace, respectfully donating art to womanhood. That’s what I feel like ‘She Belongs to Me’ is, in a similar vein.

To sing it as a woman in front of people, in front of young girls, in front of even elderly men who maybe have never had the epiphany of what it could be like for their daughter or granddaughter or wife or mother to have experienced the things that we’ve repeatedly tried to ask someone to listen to, and just to be on our team. I really love singing that song. Sometimes it’s hard because as a woman, sometimes you do feel very alone. There’s the occasion when I’ve been singing that song, sometimes I do feel very alone.

I just hope that everybody knows, hey man, I don’t write this song, but I feel really powerful singing it. I hope that the women that receive it and the men that receive it, non-binary, everybody that receives it, understands how I feel when I’m singing. I feel like we are all capable of powerful love and creative, positive nature. I love that song. I love that he wrote that song. It’s beautiful.

[Music]

Host: Chan, when we spoke to you back in 2018, it was around the Wanderer album release when you came into Triple R. We spoke about archetypes such as the wanderer, talking about some different perspectives as well. With that album you were going back to the archetype of the teller of the tale, which Dylan represents. It occurred to us, this recording and this tour, is that also a way of honouring the importance of that archetype? Is that how you see it?

Chan: Well, it’s interesting you brought that up. I think back then, at that time, 2018, I definitely had struggled through getting dropped by my label, being a single mum, and then suddenly, oh well, now I’m dropped from my label. There’s a lot of things that kind of didn’t occur to me at the time. My son’s nine years old now. He’s going to be ten in April. Having all that time to ruminate, wow, I really did get dropped from a label when I became a mother.

Some of the things that, when you’re going through certain strifes in life, you don’t have time to sort of— you’ve got to pack up and run. You’ve got to do your best in that moment. I think as we get older, I feel like we get better and we get calmer, we get wiser. That’s just how I feel. We take better care of ourselves. We know ourselves better.

That period of time, being the teller of the tale, I think all my records have always kind of been on my own. I know I’ve gotten musical support from great musicians and I’ve been very lucky in that way. But I do think that I have always been kind of doing these songs as somebody who definitely respects the singer of the song. That’s sometimes what makes a favourite song a favourite song for me. It can be sung by ten different people, the same song. You both and anyone listening will know what I’m talking about. You can have one song and it’s sung by a lot of people, but there’s always going to be that artist like Dylan, Billie Holiday or Willie Nelson. There’s always going to be that artist, Nina Simone, the singer becomes the song. ‘I love that song. Oh, Patsy Cline’s version.’

I think that that’s what Bob does, even with his own material. You love that sort of magic that someone, when they do a cover, ‘Oh wow, this is so different, and my heart is expanding because of the way this person’s vibrato sounds, just the [Unclear audio at 00:23:05–00:23:07]. It’s so different, and it’s moving me to tears and opening my soul.’ That’s just the singer, right? So Bob has both. You can hear his lyrics and his voice. It’s like his truth, the teller, the tale. Every time I hear Bob singing, it just sounds like the truth. I’m not saying I’m Bob Dylan or Billie Holiday, but me singing Bob Dylan’s song is like an homage to that feeling of having deep love for the teller of the tale, the singer of the song, even though these happen to be his songs.

Host: I guess it’s also interesting when you look at songs as moments in time, the recordings capturing a particular spark or an electricity that happens at that moment in history. Which I suppose very much relates to the recordings that you’ve made of the Royal Albert Hall, which in a way is an honouring of a legendary performance by Bob Dylan, but also a way to deepen the story yet again and add another layer, multiple layers, to its history and its meaning.

Chan: Just to move it on down the line. The world is getting more f’d up every moment. It’s just a way, like a conveyor belt, okay, let’s do this. Like you’re saying, moments in time, a spark. Who knows, maybe someone down the line will, like this movie, the dang movie that just came out with Timothée Chalamet, you know what I’m saying?

Host: Have you seen that yet?

Chan: I haven’t. I’m a real snob about movie theatres. I need to sit in a movie theatre, and I have my son. We could talk about this at length, but he doesn’t want to see the movie because I’ve been on tour with Bob Dylan’s songs. He’s kind of like, ‘Oh, you want me to sit in a movie and watch a movie about Bob, since you’ve been away from me for a year? No, I don’t want to see the movie.’ So I haven’t gotten a moment to actually go see it. But I’m going to see it eventually, of course.

But you know what I’m saying? What the fuck did I do the record for? What did I do the tour? What did I do it for, if it’s already a thing? You know what I mean? I don’t know if I wasted my time.

Host: Not at all.

Chan: But you see what I’m saying?

Host: From one perspective, it’s a celebration of the recordings, and it’s, as you say—

Chan: [Unclear audio at 00:25:35–00:25:37] I think that he just went electric because we’ve got to wake everybody up, that the time is happening, things are changing. Maybe I’m just putting my ideas in that moment of time, but it was crazy, just like it is right now, the things going on in America. That’s why I wanted to do that concert, because things were so messed up at the time. Abortion was deemed illegal. There was so much going on in America when I was like, ‘Do it, let’s just go, let’s just do this. Let’s just go do it.’

Because I thought, I’ve tried, I’m not very good academically. I wish I could be President of the United States. It ain’t gonna happen in my lifetime. I tried doing well in high school, didn’t work out. I have ADHD. I’m not really good with concentrating. I’m just not a good student. Let me just do these songs. Maybe it’ll trigger people from the past memory. Maybe they’ll remember. It’s like a testament. Bob’s still alive, running around, making great work still.

I see this movie coming out and it’s a direct hit. It’s got amazing ratings. Timothée Chalamet just came out with the soundtrack of all the songs he recorded live. He recorded all these songs. So in a way, I feel like I didn’t waste my time. I love Bob so much, and I definitely would have done this no matter what. But I worked so hard on the year of touring. It’s my job. That’s how I earn a living, is touring. We all, I guess, second-guess ourselves, and that’s human nature. I just hope that it wasn’t for nothing.

With the state the world is, I’m not saying putting out a record of when Bob Dylan went electric is going to change the world. But I just don’t know what to do, as an artist. When I get home from this Australian thing, I’ve already been recording, I’ve already been starting my next record. I guess that’s what we just have to keep doing.
